entries.title: Arabic at a glance
body: Arabic is a Semitic language written from right to left. Most words are built from a root of three consonants that carries a core meaning, shaped by patterns of vowels and extra letters.

Modern Standard Arabic (al-fuṣḥā) is used in writing, news and formal speech across the Arab world. Everyday speech uses regional dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine or Gulf Arabic, which differ a lot from each other and from the standard.

entries.title: Letter forms
entries.body: The alphabet has 28 letters, all consonants or long vowels. Letters join to their neighbours within a word, so most have four shapes depending on position: isolated, initial, medial and final.

entries.title: Letters that don't join forward
entries.body: Six letters connect to the letter before them but never to the one after, so they leave a small gap in the word. The letter that follows them takes its initial or isolated form.

examples.t: ا د ذ ر ز و
examples.r: alif · dāl · dhāl · rāʾ · zāy · wāw

examples.e: house: none of these letters join forward

entries.title: Short vowel marks
entries.body: Short vowels are written as small marks above or below a letter. Everyday texts leave them out and readers supply them from knowledge; the Qurʾan, children's books and textbooks show them.

examples.e: he wrote, without and with vowel marks

entries.title: Tāʾ marbūṭa, alif maqṣūra and hamza
body: {ة} (tāʾ marbūṭa) appears only at the end of a word and usually marks a feminine noun. It is said as -a, but as -at when a word follows in a possessive phrase.
{ى} (alif maqṣūra) is an ā at the end of a word written with a dotless yāʾ.
{ء} (hamza) is a glottal stop. It sits alone or on a carrier letter: أ إ ؤ ئ.

a gargled r, like French r

entries.title: The article al- and sun letters
body: The definite article is {ال} (al-), written joined to the noun. Before the 14 sun letters, made with the tongue tip, the l is not said and the next consonant is doubled instead. Before moon letters, the l is said.
Sun letters: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن. The spelling never changes, only the sound.

examples.e: the sun (sun letter: the l assimilates)
the moon (moon letter: the l is pronounced)

entries.title: Roots and patterns
entries.body: Learn a root and you can guess dozens of words. The root k-t-b is about writing; patterns turn it into a place, a person, an object or an action.

examples.e: written; a letter (pattern maCCūC: done to)

entries.title: Sentences without is
entries.body: In the present tense Arabic has no verb to be. A definite subject followed by an indefinite word makes a complete sentence. If both are definite, it is a phrase: the big house.

entries.title: Gender and agreement
entries.body: Nouns are masculine or feminine; ة usually marks feminine. Adjectives follow the noun and match it in gender, number and definiteness. Plurals of things (not people) take feminine singular adjectives.

examples.e: new cars (non-human plural takes feminine singular)

entries.title: Personal pronouns and possessive endings
entries.body: You is different for a man and a woman. Possession is a suffix on the noun.

entries.title: Past and present: katab, yaktub
entries.body: The past tense adds suffixes to the stem; the present adds prefixes (and some suffixes). The basic word order in formal Arabic is verb, subject, object, but subject first is also common.

entries.title: Numbers and digits
body: Many Arab countries write digits in the Eastern Arabic form. Numbers are written left to right even inside right-to-left text: ٢٠٢٦ is 2026.
The words for 3 to 10 take the opposite gender ending to the noun they count, one of the famous quirks of Arabic grammar.

examples.e: God willing. (said of anything in the future)
